name: The Zybach Collection
subtitle: The life's work of Dr. Bob Zybach: Oregon forest history, oral history and historical ecology

series.title: Soap Creek Valley Oral History Series
series.summary: Fifteen printed oral-history monographs recorded in Soap Creek Valley, Benton County, Oregon between 1989 and 2009 by Bob Zybach and colleagues for Oregon State University Research Forests, with the 1989 Historic Soap Creek Valley Auto Tour and the 1999 M.A.I.S. thesis that draws on them. Narrators were born between 1890 and 1930; each transcript was reviewed and approved by its narrator and printed with its own back index.

series.title: Elliott State Forest oral histories, field trips and videos
series.summary: The Elliott State Forest 2017–2019 Oral History Project: six recorded interviews and driving tours with Jerry Phillips, David Gould, Bob Jacobson, Roger Johnson and Gary Vonderohe, interviewed by Bob Zybach with Amber Ross and Randy Wiest, indexed by tape side and minute. Filed with them are earlier Herman Larson recordings, OSU SCARC Jacobson transcripts, the ORWW photograph, map and MP3 registers, and the ORWWmedia video playlist.

series.title: Alberta Street
series.summary: The 1992 Alberta Street Cultural Resource Inventory in North/Northeast Portland, researched by Portland African American high-school students, and the 2015 replication that updated its methods and recommendations. Published by ORWW as the 2015 Alberta Street Project, with a chapter history of the neighbourhood from the Chinookan villages to 2015 gentrification, cultural-resource inventories, maps and public-safety and education sections.
summary_basis: ORWW home page project listing, '2015 1992 Alberta Street Project Revisited'
series.described_from: public ORWW project pages; no files accessioned in the 2026 upload

series.title: The Osbornes Project
series.summary: Western Oregon Osborne photographs, 1932–1940: panoramic photographs taken from 1930s fire lookouts, collected across four earlier ORWW projects (2004, 2006, 2007, 2010) and consolidated in 2020 by county, with Benton, Lane, Lincoln and Polk counties added. Used for repeat photography and forest-cover comparison.
summary_basis: ORWW home page project listing, '2020 Western Oregon Osborne Photos, 1932-1940'
series.described_from: public ORWW project pages; no files accessioned in the 2026 upload

series.title: Jedediah Smith and the 1828 Umpqua Memorial
series.summary: The 1828 Umpqua Memorial Project: the record of the 14 July 1828 attack in which beaver trappers travelling under Jedediah Smith were killed near the mouth of the Smith River in Douglas County, Oregon, and of the burial of eleven of them that October by a Hudson’s Bay Company brigade; and the record of a modern project, run by Bob Zybach for Oregon Websites and Watershed Project, Inc. and the Jedediah Smith Society between 2000 and 2023, to replace a state highway marker, raise a memorial stone and hold a four-day rendezvous over the route of 1828. Eleven of the creator’s writings are published page by page, with the 1828 primary sources, the reference shelf, the markers, the guidebooks, the maps and the photograph registers. No content that would locate the attack, the Kelawatset village or the graves is published.
series.described_from: the creator's own published project site at orww.org/1828_Umpqua_Memorial/, 375 files in 36 folders, read 4 September 2026

series.title: Letitia Carson, 1824–1922
series.summary: Letitia Carson was born enslaved in Kentucky between 1814 and 1818, crossed the Oregon Trail in 1845, and settled with David Carson on a claim in Soap Creek Valley. After his death in 1852 she sued the administrator of his estate twice and won both times, and in 1868 she proved a homestead claim on South Myrtle Creek in her own name. The series is the primary record the creator has assembled and published — citizenship papers, two probate files, the case file of Carson v. Smith, the homestead file — with the transcriptions made from it, his own writing about her from 1989 to 2016, his photographs of the ground, and the maps.
series.described_from: the creator's own published pages at orww.org, mirrored and described item by item

series.title: Wildfire and Oregon forest fire history
series.summary: Western Oregon forest fire history, 1765 to 2022: the ORWW educational wildfire websites (2004 B&B Complex, 2005 Deer Creek, 2007 Southwestern Oregon, 2008 Biscuit, 2009 Wildfire Economic, 2016 Douglas Fir Region) and the 2020 Labor Day Fires documentation. Based on Dr. Zybach's 2003 PhD dissertation, The Great Fires.
summary_basis: ORWW home page project listing, '2022 Western Oregon Forest Fire History, 1765 to 2022'
series.described_from: public ORWW project pages; no files accessioned in the 2026 upload

rights.statement: Working edition, 2026. The Library publishes this collection with the creator's participation while rights and consultation reviews continue. The monographs were published by Oregon State University Research Forests and College of Forestry and are published by the creator on his own site; narrator releases ran to OSU Research Forests and to the Horner Museum (now the Benton County Historical Society). The creator retains all rights he holds; the Library's indexes, place and people pages and timeline are the Library's own work. Rights are stated series by series at /collections/zybach/rights/, which also says how to ask for a change or removal.
rights.note: Rights are not settled: no deed of gift has been executed, and the Soap Creek monographs were published by OSU Research Forests and the College of Forestry, which funded the project. Nothing here asserts who holds copyright.

per_series.statement: Printed monographs published by Oregon State University Research Forests and College of Forestry; the transcripts were reviewed and approved by their narrators. Displayed here for education and research, with attribution. Originals remain at the creator's site.

Recordings, transcripts, photographs and maps published by Oregon Websites and Watershed Project, Inc. (ORWW); videos published on the ORWWmedia YouTube channel. Displayed here for education and research, with attribution. Media are linked at their originals, not copied.

creator.bio_source_note: Draft text carried over from the demonstration finding aid at src/pages/collections/zybach.astro ('About the creator'). Not written or approved by Dr. Zybach.
creator.bio_text: Dr. Zybach is a historical ecologist and Oregon forest-history researcher. His current public project pages are at orww.store, and the long-running Oregon Websites and Watersheds archive is at orww.org.

what_the_fleet_did: Fetched the public PDFs, photographs, maps and MP3 link registers from nwmapsco.com and orww.org, and recorded a SHA-256 checksum for every file read.
Read each printed monograph page by page with pdftotext, keeping the printed page number as the citation unit and recording the PDF-to-printed page rule used.
Recovered speaker turns from the printed typography, and marked every attribution that was inferred rather than printed.
Rebuilt the series index from the fifteen printed back indexes, merged headings, and resolved page references to chapters.
Assembled place, person and chronology authorities from the records, geocoding place names against USGS GNIS where a match existed.
Consolidated the readers' content notes with an independent pattern scan, and kept only high and medium severity notes for display.
Generated this site's data files from those records, applying the holds and the withheld-place policy.
what_it_did_not_do: It did not paraphrase, summarise or rewrite any narrator's or the creator's prose; quoted text is character-for-character from the page.
It did not correct content. Only obvious OCR artefacts were fixed, and every fix is recorded with page and before/after.
It did not invent missing values. Fields that could not be filled from the document are null and listed in gaps.
It did not decide the sensitive questions: content notes, holds and withheld places are flagged for human decision, not resolved.
It did not verify coordinates in the field; a coordinate carries its method and confidence.
